targets.title: Learning new response sequences.
targets.evidence_quote: The present study replicated Reid’s work using human participants and a tabletop game called PORTL.
targets.outcome_quote: Similar to Reid, participants were periodically shifted to a new target sequence that differed in either the first or last position. The present study also found that acquisition of the new sequence generally occurred more rapidly when the shift was in the last position, and more errors occurred when the change was in the first position.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The author explicitly reports the same acquisition/error asymmetry as Reid. An alternative explanation in terms of learned movement patterns challenges the theoretical interpretation, without rejecting the replicated central empirical pattern or declaring the methods invalid.

reasoning: A human PORTL experiment retests Reid’s published rat response-sequence finding. Other theories and historical examples are explanatory comparisons, not additional findings deliberately retested. The thesis title page dates it December 2024; repository accession in 2025 explains the supplied year discrepancy without an identity mismatch.
